Question #1
```{r}
#a.
S_Size <- c(6.5, 9.0, 8.5, 8.5, 10.5, 7.0, 9.5, 9.0, 13.0, 7.5, 10.5, 8.5, 12.0, 10.5,
13.0, 11.5, 8.5, 5.0, 10.0, 6.5, 7.5, 8.5, 10.5, 8.5, 10.5, 11.0, 9.0, 13.0)
Height <- c(66.0, 68.0, 64.5, 65.0, 70.0, 64.0, 70.0, 71.0, 72.0, 64.0, 74.5, 67.0, 71.0, 71.0,
77.0, 72.0, 59.0, 62.0, 72.0, 66.0, 64.0, 67.0, 73.0, 69.0, 72.0, 70.0, 69.0, 70.0)
Gender <- c("F", "F", "F", "F", "M", "F", "F", "F", "M", "F", "M", "F", "M", "M",
"M", "M", "F", "F", "M", "F", "F", "M", "M", "F", "M", "M", "M", "M")

shoesize <- data.frame(S_size = S_Size, Height = Height, Gender = Gender)
write.csv(shoesize, "shoesize.csv", row.names = FALSE)

#b.
shoe <-read.csv("shoesize.csv")
tail(shoe,5)

#c.
str(shoe)

#d.
dim(shoe)
nrow(shoe)
ncol(shoe)

#e.
summary(shoe)
#str shows the data's structure such as rows and columns. 
#While sumary gives the min mean median etc.

#f.
males   <- shoe[shoe$Gender == "M", c("S_size", "Height")]
females <- shoe[shoe$Gender == "F", c("S_size", "Height")]
males
females

#g.
mean(shoe$S_size)
mean(shoe$Height)

#h.
#Yes,Taller people tend to have bigger shoe sizes.
```

Question #4
```{r}
str(shoe)
#Gender imports as chr, which is expected since read.csv() doesn't create factors by default. If #ShoeSize were accidentally imported as text, mean() would return NA, sorting would go #alphabetically, and plots and models wouldn't treat it as numeric, so you'd need to clean the bad #value and use as.numeric().
```

Question #7
```{r}
mean(females$Height)
mean(males$Height)
mean(females$S_size)
mean(males$S_size)

# The male subset has a higher mean than the female subset on both height and shoe size.
# This supports the claim that shoe size and height are related. Since males also tend
# to be taller than females, gender should be accounted for when studying the relationship.
```
